title: Sequence and Series
notes: **Sequence and series.** A sequence is an ordered list a₁, a₂, a₃, … whose nth term aₙ is a function of the positive integer n; the series is the sum a₁ + a₂ + … + aₙ, written Σaₙ.
**Arithmetic progression.** Consecutive terms differ by a constant d, so aₙ = a + (n − 1)d and Sₙ = n/2[2a + (n − 1)d] = n/2(a + l), where l is the last term.
**Geometric progression.** Consecutive terms have a constant ratio r, so aₙ = arⁿ⁻¹ and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1; the infinite sum S∞ = a/(1 − r) exists only when |r| < 1.
**Worked example.** In 3, 7, 11, … the common difference is 4, hence a₂₀ = 3 + 19·4 = 79 and S₂₀ = 20/2(3 + 79) = 820.
**Means.** For positive a and b the arithmetic mean is (a + b)/2 and the geometric mean is √(ab); AM ≥ GM always, with equality only when a = b.
**Exam caution.** Count the number of terms from the first and last indices before applying Sₙ, and check r = 1 separately because the GP sum formula divides by 1 − r.
summary: A sequence is an ordered list governed by a rule for its nth term; a series is the sum of those terms. Arithmetic, geometric and special sums each have their own closed form.
